text:
María Guadalupe Sánchez Ramírez, conocida en casa como Lupita. Fecha de nacimiento: July 10, 2022. Edad cronológica al momento de esta evaluación: 4;2 (años;meses). Fecha de la evaluación: September 15, 2026, con sesión de seguimiento el September 18, 2026. Lugar de la evaluación: domicilio familiar en 4417 Persimmon Creek Lane, Durham, 27705, Durham County. Agencia que refiere y coordina servicios: CDSA del Piamonte Central. Coordinadora de servicios: Patricia Gómez. Intérprete certificada de español médico: Rosa Elena Pacheco. Patóloga del habla y lenguaje bilingüe, evaluadora: Mariana Castillo Vega, M.S., CCC-SLP, de Carolina Speech & Language Partners, PLLC. Número de expediente: CDSA-2026-04871. Número de identificación de Medicaid: 584217693B. Teléfono de contacto de la familia: (919) 555-0148. Correo electrónico de la clínica: mcastillo@carolinaspeechpartners.com.

Este informe documenta la evaluación integral del habla y el lenguaje de Lupita, realizada a solicitud de la pediatra de la niña, la Dra. Susana Marín, del consultorio de Duke Children's Primary Care, después de que los padres expresaran preocupación por el desarrollo del lenguaje expresivo y por dificultades de articulación que afectan la inteligibilidad del habla de su hija tanto en español como en inglés. La evaluación se llevó a cabo en el hogar familiar, en presencia de la madre, Alejandra Ramírez Flores, y con apoyo de la intérprete Rosa Elena Pacheco, quien facilitó la comunicación entre esta evaluadora y la familia durante toda la sesión, dado que la madre se siente más cómoda expresando detalles clínicos complejos en español. El padre, Eduardo Sánchez Vidal, participó por teléfono desde su trabajo en Cardinal Logistics Management durante la porción de la entrevista relacionada con la historia familiar.

Lupita es la segunda de dos hijos. Su hermano mayor, José Antonio Sánchez Ramírez, a quien todos llaman Pepe, tiene 7 años y asiste a segundo grado sin dificultades académicas reportadas. Según la madre, Pepe habla por su hermana con frecuencia en situaciones sociales, lo cual, según refiere la familia, puede estar reduciendo las oportunidades de que Lupita practique la expresión verbal de manera independiente. La familia cuenta además con el apoyo frecuente de la abuela materna, Teodora Flores Nuñez, a quien la niña llama cariñosamente "Teo", quien cuida a Lupita dos tardes por semana mientras los padres trabajan. Otra cuidadora habitual es la vecina y niñera de la familia, Carmen Rosales, quien ha estado al cuidado de la niña desde los 18 meses de edad y conoce bien sus rutinas de comunicación. Durante la entrevista, la madre mencionó también a dos primos que pasan mucho tiempo con Lupita los fines de semana: Juan Carlos Ramírez Ortiz, a quien llaman "Juanito", de 6 años, y su hermano Jesús Ramírez Ortiz, apodado "Chuy", de 9 años; ambos primos suelen jugar con la niña y, según la madre, Lupita los imita mucho en su forma de hablar. La familia tiene además un perro llamado Rocky, que la niña menciona con frecuencia en sus juegos y que, según refieren los padres, es una de las motivaciones favoritas para que la niña intente producir enunciados más largos ("Rocky quiere agua", "Rocky se sentó").

Historia prenatal, de nacimiento y médica: el embarazo de Lupita fue de término completo, sin complicaciones reportadas por la madre. El parto fue vaginal, sin asistencia instrumental, y ocurrió en el Duke Regional Hospital el July 10, 2022. El peso al nacer fue de 7 libras y 4 onzas, y la niña no requirió ingreso a la unidad de cuidados intensivos neonatales. No se reportan hospitalizaciones posteriores de importancia, aunque la madre indica que Lupita tuvo varios episodios de otitis media entre los 10 y los 24 meses de edad, tratados con antibióticos por su pediatra. Se colocaron tubos de ventilación (miringotomía bilateral) a los 2;3 años, procedimiento realizado en Duke Regional Hospital bajo el cuidado del otorrinolaringólogo del equipo. Desde entonces, la madre reporta una notable disminución en la frecuencia de infecciones de oído. La audición de la niña fue evaluada formalmente por audiología pediátrica en March 3, 2025, con resultados dentro de límites normales bilateralmente, documentados con timpanometría tipo A en ambos oídos.

Lupita recibe actualmente terapia ocupacional a través del programa de intervención temprana, con la terapeuta Katherine Nguyen, OTR/L, quien trabaja principalmente en el área de integración sensorial y coordinación motora fina, y terapia física con David Whitfield, PT, DPT, debido a un retraso leve en hitos motores gruesos observado durante el primer año de vida. Ambos terapeutas han colaborado con esta evaluadora para coordinar objetivos compartidos, particularmente en lo relacionado con la planificación motora oral y la postura durante las actividades de alimentación, que según los reportes de terapia ocupacional pueden estar relacionadas con algunas de las dificultades articulatorias observadas.

Historia familiar y de lenguaje: en el hogar se habla principalmente español, idioma que ambos padres consideran su lengua dominante y en el que se comunican entre ellos y con los abuelos. El padre, Eduardo Sánchez Vidal, trabaja en inglés en su empleo y reporta sentirse cómodo en ambos idiomas, mientras que la madre, Alejandra Ramírez Flores, que trabaja medio tiempo desde casa, prefiere comunicarse en español en la mayoría de los contextos. Lupita asiste de lunes a viernes, de 8:00 a.m. a 3:30 p.m., al centro Centro de Cuidado Infantil Pequeños Pasos, donde la instrucción se imparte principalmente en inglés. Su maestra principal, la Srta. Brenda Collazo, reporta que Lupita es una niña sociable que participa en actividades grupales, pero que con frecuencia recurre a gestos y a señalar objetos cuando no logra producir las palabras que busca en inglés. En el salón, sus compañeras más cercanas son Emily y Santiago, con quienes juega casi todos los días y de quienes, según la maestra, Lupita ha comenzado a imitar frases cortas en inglés durante el juego libre.

Los padres describen a Lupita como una niña cariñosa, curiosa y persistente, que disfruta de los libros ilustrados, de cantar canciones infantiles y de jugar a "la cocinita" con su abuela Teodora Flores Nuñez. Sin embargo, ambos padres coinciden en que su hija es notablemente menos inteligible que otros niños de su edad, tanto para familiares cercanos como para personas fuera del círculo familiar, incluyendo a la maestra Brenda Collazo y a la niñera Carmen Rosales, quienes en ocasiones piden que la madre "traduzca" lo que dice la niña.

Observación conductual: durante la sesión de evaluación, Lupita se mostró inicialmente tímida, pero se calentó rápidamente al ambiente de juego estructurado, utilizando figuras de animales y un pequeño set de cocina como apoyo para la elicitación de lenguaje. Mantuvo buen contacto visual, atención compartida adecuada para su edad y disfrutó de los turnos conversacionales cuando el vocabulario le resultaba familiar. Se observaron varios episodios de frustración leve cuando la niña intentaba comunicar una idea más compleja y no lograba ser comprendida de inmediato por esta evaluadora ni por la intérprete, momento en el cual recurría a gestos, a señalar, o a buscar la mirada de su madre para que interviniera.

Resultados de las pruebas: se administraron instrumentos estandarizados en español, complementados con muestra de lenguaje espontáneo e inventario articulatorio informal, dado que la familia reporta exposición dominante al español en el hogar. Se utilizó el Preschool Language Scale-5 Spanish Edition (PLS-5 Spanish), el Clinical Evaluation of Language Fundamentals Preschool-3 Spanish (CELF Preschool-3 Spanish) para el componente de seguimiento de instrucciones, y el Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation-3 (GFTA-3) con transcripción fonética adaptada para contrastar patrones en ambos idiomas. Se recogió además una muestra de lenguaje espontáneo de 50 enunciados, codificada en formato SALT, en la cual se observaron varios ejemplos de omisión de palabra final, codificados como [EW] en la transcripción.

Los resultados se resumen en la siguiente tabla:

Prueba — Puntuación estándar — Percentil — Rango descriptivo
PLS-5 Spanish, Lenguaje Auditivo — 76 — 5 — Por debajo del promedio
PLS-5 Spanish, Lenguaje Expresivo — 71 — 3 — Muy por debajo del promedio
PLS-5 Spanish, Puntuación Total — 73 — 4 — Muy por debajo del promedio
CELF Preschool-3 Spanish, Seguimiento de Instrucciones — 82 — 12 — Dentro de límites bajos
GFTA-3, Puntuación Estándar de Sonidos en Palabras — 68 — 2 — Muy por debajo del promedio

En la prueba de lenguaje receptivo, Lupita obtuvo una puntuación estándar de 76 (percentil 5), lo que indica un desempeño por debajo del promedio esperado para su edad en la comprensión de vocabulario, conceptos relacionales y seguimiento de instrucciones de dos y tres pasos en español. En la subprueba de lenguaje expresivo, obtuvo una puntuación estándar de 71 (percentil 3), con dificultades evidentes en la formulación de oraciones completas, en el uso de marcadores morfológicos de tiempo verbal (por ejemplo, omitió consistentemente la terminación verbal al narrar acciones pasadas) y en la producción de vocabulario descriptivo. La puntuación total del PLS-5 Spanish fue de 73 (percentil 4), ubicando su desempeño general de lenguaje muy por debajo del promedio esperado para su edad cronológica.

En el área articulatoria, el GFTA-3 arrojó una puntuación estándar de 68 (percentil 2). Se observaron sustituciones consistentes de /r/ por [w] en posición intervocálica e inicial ("[w]osa" por "rosa"), simplificación de grupos consonánticos (por ejemplo, "pache" por "parche"), y procesos de posteriorización velar ocasionales. En inglés, se observó un patrón similar en los sonidos /r/ y /s/, con sustitución parcial de /s/ por [θ] en posición inicial de palabra. La inteligibilidad global se estimó en aproximadamente 40% para oyentes no familiarizados y en torno a 70% para oyentes familiares, en contextos de oración completa sin apoyo de contexto situacional. Durante tareas de imitación directa con apoyo visual y claves táctiles (mod cues), Lupita logró producir correctamente el sonido /r/ en 8/10 ensayos, lo cual sugiere buen potencial de respuesta a la intervención con niveles moderados de apoyo.

En la muestra de lenguaje espontáneo, la longitud media de enunciado fue de aproximadamente 3.1 morfemas, por debajo de lo esperado para su edad. Se observaron enunciados tales como "Lupita quiere jugo", "Rocky no" y "mamá, upa", con omisión frecuente de artículos y de conjugaciones verbales completas. No se observaron ecolalias ni estereotipias verbales. La comprensión de preguntas con "qué" y "dónde" fue consistente, mientras que las preguntas con "por qué" y "cuándo" resultaron considerablemente más difíciles, con respuestas frecuentemente fuera de tema.

Impresiones diagnósticas: con base en los resultados obtenidos en ambas áreas de lenguaje receptivo y expresivo, en la historia de desarrollo reportada por la familia, y en la observación clínica directa, esta evaluadora concluye que Lupita presenta un trastorno mixto del lenguaje receptivo-expresivo (ICD-10: F80.2), de severidad moderada, junto con un trastorno fonológico concomitante que afecta de manera significativa la inteligibilidad del habla en ambos idiomas, español e inglés. El perfil observado es consistente con un patrón de desarrollo bilingüe típico combinado con un retraso de lenguaje subyacente, y no se atribuye únicamente a la exposición a dos idiomas. La historia de otitis media recurrente durante el período crítico de desarrollo fonológico (10 a 24 meses) es un factor contribuyente probable, aunque no explica por completo la magnitud del retraso observado en ambas áreas de lenguaje. Se recomienda continuar monitoreando la audición de manera periódica dado este historial.

Dada la naturaleza bilingüe del hogar y del entorno educativo de la niña, se recomienda enfáticamente que la intervención se realice en ambos idiomas, priorizando el español como lengua de instrucción inicial dado que es la lengua dominante del hogar, con generalización planificada hacia el inglés conforme avancen las habilidades en español. Esta evaluación se codifica bajo el procedimiento CPT 92523 (evaluación de producción del habla con evaluación del lenguaje).

Recomendaciones: se recomienda que Lupita reciba terapia de habla y lenguaje individual dos veces por semana, con sesiones de 30 a 45 minutos, idealmente proporcionadas por un terapeuta bilingüe o, en su defecto, con apoyo consistente de intérprete calificado como Rosa Elena Pacheco durante cada sesión. Los objetivos terapéuticos deben incluir: aumento de la longitud media de enunciado mediante estrategias de expansión y modelado en ambos idiomas; mejora de la producción de /r/ y de los grupos consonánticos en posición inicial y media de palabra mediante un enfoque de intervención fonológica basado en contrastes mínimos; y fortalecimiento de la comprensión de preguntas de "por qué" y "cuándo" mediante actividades narrativas con apoyo visual.

Se recomienda además que la familia continúe coordinando de cerca con la coordinadora de servicios Patricia Gómez de CDSA del Piamonte Central para la actualización del Plan Individualizado de Servicios para la Familia (IFSP), con fecha de revisión programada para el December 10, 2026. Se sugiere mantener comunicación regular con la maestra Brenda Collazo en Centro de Cuidado Infantil Pequeños Pasos para reforzar estrategias de lenguaje en el entorno de aula, incluyendo el uso de apoyo visual y la validación de los intentos comunicativos de la niña aunque no sean completamente inteligibles. Se recomienda también continuar la coordinación interdisciplinaria con la terapeuta ocupacional Katherine Nguyen y el fisioterapeuta David Whitfield, dado el posible componente de planificación motora oral identificado en esta evaluación, así como mantener informada a la pediatra, Dra. Susana Marín, sobre el seguimiento audiológico recomendado.

En el hogar, se anima a los padres, Alejandra Ramírez Flores y Eduardo Sánchez Vidal, así como a la abuela Teodora Flores Nuñez y a la niñera Carmen Rosales, a continuar narrando actividades cotidianas en voz alta en español, a expandir los enunciados de la niña en lugar de corregir directamente sus errores de pronunciación, y a aprovechar el interés de Lupita por su perro Rocky y por el juego con sus primos Juanito y Chuy como contextos motivadores para practicar enunciados más largos. Se sugiere limitar las ocasiones en que Pepe hable en nombre de su hermana, fomentando en su lugar que espere pacientemente a que Lupita intente comunicar su mensaje de forma independiente antes de intervenir.

Se recomienda una reevaluación formal en un período de seis meses para medir progreso en ambas áreas de lenguaje y en inteligibilidad del habla, y se recomienda repetir la evaluación audiológica anualmente dado el historial de otitis media. Esta evaluadora permanece disponible para coordinar con todos los proveedores mencionados y con la familia para asegurar la continuidad de cuidados. Informe elaborado y firmado por Mariana Castillo Vega, M.S., CCC-SLP, Carolina Speech & Language Partners, PLLC, el September 22, 2026.

CAROLINA BILINGUAL SPEECH & LANGUAGE SERVICES, PLLC
2210 Tate Boulevard SE, Hickory, NC 28602

SPEECH-LANGUAGE EVALUATION REPORT

Client Name: María José Fernández López
Preferred Name: Majo
Date of Birth: March 3, 2022
Age at Evaluation: 4;6
Evaluation Date: September 15, 2026
Report Date: September 22, 2026
Sex: Female
Primary Language(s): Spanish (home), English (daycare/preschool)

Mother: Daniela López
Father: Carlos Fernández
Address: 142 Maple Hollow Drive, Hickory, Catawba County, NC 28601
Home Phone: (828) 555-0192

Medicaid ID: 584213769B
Insurance (BCBSNC) Member ID: ZNC48827135
NC ITP Child ID: ITP-2022-04471
Authorization/Record Number: 2026-77821-SLP
Referral Source: Western Piedmont CDSA, Service Coordinator Whitney Brooks
Evaluating Clinician: Jennifer Hayes, M.S., CCC-SLP

1. REASON FOR REFERRAL

María José (“Majo”) was referred for a comprehensive bilingual speech-language evaluation by Western Piedmont CDSA service coordinator Whitney Brooks, following a request from her mother, Daniela López, and her daycare teacher, Miss Ana, at Little Sprouts Early Learning Center. Reported concerns include limited intelligibility in both Spanish and English, an expressive vocabulary that appears smaller than that of same-age classmates, and difficulty following two- and three-step directions in the classroom. Mrs. López also reports that Majo is sometimes difficult to understand even for close family members, including her maternal grandmother, doña Lupe, who cares for Majo most weekday mornings before daycare drop-off.

This evaluation was completed to describe Majo's current receptive and expressive language skills and speech sound production in both of her languages, to inform transition planning from the Western Piedmont CDSA Infant-Toddler Program, and to generate recommendations as she prepares to move into a public preschool classroom.

2. BACKGROUND INFORMATION

2.1 Birth and Medical History

Majo was born on March 3, 2022, at Piedmont Regional Medical Center in Hickory, following a full-term pregnancy and an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. Birth weight was 7 lbs., 4 oz. Mrs. López reported no pregnancy complications and no NICU stay. Majo's pediatrician, Dr. Rebecca Simmons, has followed her since birth and reports that gross motor milestones and physical growth have been age-appropriate throughout.

Medical history is significant for recurrent otitis media. Majo had six documented ear infections between 10 months and 2;8, culminating in bilateral myringotomy tube placement on January 14, 2025 by Dr. Imran Patel. Mrs. López reports that Majo's listening and attending behaviors improved noticeably after the tubes were placed, though mild residual fluid was noted at a well-check on August 3, 2026. A follow-up audiogram completed on August 10, 2026 documented hearing within normal limits bilaterally, with normal tympanometric results in both ears. No other hospitalizations, surgeries, or significant medical events were reported. Majo takes no current medications.

2.2 Developmental History

Per Mrs. López, Majo's gross and fine motor development have progressed within typical limits; she walked independently at 13 months and currently runs, climbs stairs, and holds crayons and utensils appropriately for her age. Early communication milestones were somewhat delayed: first words emerged around 20 months, noticeably later than her older brother, Mateo Fernández López, now 6 years old and enrolled at Oakwood Elementary School.

Majo began attending Little Sprouts Early Learning Center at 18 months, first in a mixed toddler room and currently in Miss Ana's preschool classroom, four days a week from 7:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.. On the fifth weekday, Majo stays home with doña Lupe. This fall, Majo also began attending a part-time NC Pre-K classroom taught by la maestra Carmen on Tuesday and Thursday mornings from 8:45 a.m. to 11:30 a.m., prior to being dropped off at Little Sprouts Early Learning Center for the remainder of the day. Both Miss Ana and la maestra Carmen report that Majo is social and affectionate with peers but frequently relies on gesture, pointing, and single words rather than connected speech to communicate wants and needs.

2.3 Family and Language History

Majo lives with her parents, Daniela López and Carlos Fernández; her brother, Mateo Fernández López; and her maternal grandmother, doña Lupe, at the family's home on Maple Hollow Drive in Hickory. Mrs. López works at Catawba Valley Poultry Processing, typically on an early shift from 6:00 a.m. to 2:30 p.m., while Mr. Fernández works at Blue Ridge Trucking Co. and is frequently away from home for two to three days at a time. A family friend and neighbor, Mr. Tom, occasionally watches Majo and her brother in the early evening when both parents' schedules overlap.

Spanish is the primary language spoken in the home among all family members, including doña Lupe, who speaks limited English. Mr. Fernández and Mrs. López both report conversational proficiency in English, which they use primarily at work and with Majo's teachers. Mateo is described as dominant in English following two years of public school, though he continues to understand and respond to Spanish at home. Majo is reported to understand both Spanish and English reasonably well but to produce far fewer intelligible words in either language than would be expected for her age. Mrs. López estimates that, overall, Majo hears approximately 70% Spanish and 30% English input across a typical week, with English exposure concentrated at Little Sprouts Early Learning Center and in la maestra Carmen's classroom.

No other family members are reported to have a history of speech, language, or learning difficulties. The family's dog, Nico, is frequently mentioned by Majo during play and was a motivating topic throughout the evaluation.

3. ASSESSMENT PROCEDURES

This evaluation was conducted in the family's home language, Spanish, with English administered where developmentally appropriate, in order to obtain a representative picture of Majo's communication skills across both languages. The evaluation session took place on September 15, 2026, beginning at 9:15 a.m. and concluding at 11:40 a.m., with a snack and movement break from 10:20 a.m. to 10:35 a.m.. The session was conducted at the family's home on Maple Hollow Drive.

Given that Majo's parents and grandmother are primarily Spanish-speaking, certified medical interpreter Gloria Reyes was present throughout the session to support communication between the family and this examiner regarding case history, instructions, and feedback. Whitney Brooks, service coordinator with Western Piedmont CDSA, also observed the first portion of the session for transition planning purposes.

The following procedures were completed:
- Parent/caregiver interview (with interpreter support)
- Review of prior audiological and medical records
- Preschool Language Scale, Fifth Edition (PLS-5), English Edition
- Preschool Language Scale, Fifth Edition (PLS-5), Spanish Edition
- Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition (GFTA-3)
- Spontaneous speech-language samples in Spanish and English (approximately 50 utterances each)
- Oral-motor examination
- Informal play-based observation

4. BEHAVIORAL OBSERVATIONS

Majo separated easily from doña Lupe, who remained nearby during most of the session, and engaged readily with this examiner and with Ms. Reyes. She demonstrated age-appropriate joint attention, eye contact, and turn-taking during play-based tasks. Majo transitioned well between Spanish-language and English-language tasks, though she showed a clear preference for responding in Spanish and frequently code-switched mid-utterance, which is a typical and expected pattern for a bilingual child of her age and language exposure.

Attention and engagement were adequate throughout formal testing, with occasional redirection needed during the final 15 minutes of the session. Oral-motor structures and function appeared grossly within normal limits for speech; no significant structural or motor concerns were noted. Hearing was judged to be functionally adequate for testing purposes, consistent with the recent audiogram.

5. TEST RESULTS

5.1 Standardized Test Scores

| Measure | Domain | Standard Score | Percentile Rank |
|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5 (English) | Auditory Comprehension | 78 | 7th |
| PLS-5 (English) | Expressive Communication | 74 | 4th |
| PLS-5 (English) | Total Language Score | 75 | 5th |
| PLS-5 (Spanish) | Auditory Comprehension | 85 | 16th |
| PLS-5 (Spanish) | Expressive Communication | 80 | 9th |
| PLS-5 (Spanish) | Total Language Score | 81 | 10th |
| GFTA-3 | Sounds-in-Words | 72 | 3rd |

5.2 Speech Sound Production

Percentage of Consonants Correct (PCC) was calculated from spontaneous speech samples obtained in each language. In the Spanish sample, PCC was 62%; in the English sample, PCC was 58%. Error patterns were consistent across both languages and included final consonant deletion, cluster reduction, and gliding of liquids.

Examples of Majo's Spanish productions included "tete" for "leche," reflecting fronting and stopping, and "nana" for "banana," reflecting weak syllable deletion. In English, Majo produced "wabbit" for "rabbit" (gliding of /r/) and "pay" for "play" (cluster reduction). Stimulability testing showed that Majo could approximate the target /l/ in isolation with mod cues but reduced clusters again at the word level. Several target words were coded [EW] during the English sample for whole-word errors affecting intelligibility.

5.3 Intelligibility

Using a structured rating scale, Majo's connected speech was approximately 7/10 words intelligible to a familiar listener (her mother) in context, and approximately 3/10 words intelligible to an unfamiliar listener (this examiner) without contextual support, in both languages. This represents a clinically significant intelligibility deficit for a child of 4;6.

5.4 Language Sampling

Mean length of utterance in words, calculated from the Spanish sample, was 2.8 words per utterance, below expectations for her age. Majo used primarily two- and three-word combinations, with limited use of grammatical morphemes in either language (for example, plural markers and verb tense inflections were frequently omitted). Vocabulary diversity, as measured by number of different words across the combined sample, was also below expectations relative to typical peers.

6. CLINICAL IMPRESSIONS

Results of this evaluation indicate that Majo presents with a speech sound disorder and a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder affecting both of her languages, Spanish and English. Her language scores fell in the below-average to well-below-average range in both languages, with Spanish scores somewhat stronger than English scores, consistent with her relative language exposure. Because deficits are present across both languages rather than isolated to the second, non-dominant language, these findings are not accounted for by typical bilingual language-learning patterns alone and are consistent with a true underlying language impairment (ICD-10: F80.1, Expressive Language Disorder, with receptive involvement).

Majo's speech sound production also fell in the well-below-average range, with reduced intelligibility across both languages that is significant for her age and exceeds what would be expected from typical bilingual phonological development or residual effects of her history of otitis media alone (ICD-10: F80.0, Phonological Disorder). Her history of recurrent otitis media with effusion likely contributed to, though does not fully account for, her current speech and language profile, particularly given her now-normal hearing.

Majo's nonverbal communication skills, social engagement, play skills, and oral-motor function are judged to be age-appropriate and are considered relative strengths that will support her progress in intervention.

7. SUMMARY

María José Fernández López, a 4;6-year-old bilingual Spanish-English-speaking girl, was evaluated at the request of her family and daycare teacher due to concerns regarding intelligibility and expressive language. Results of standardized testing and language sampling in both Spanish and English indicate a speech sound disorder and a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder affecting both languages. Majo demonstrates relative strengths in social communication, play, and nonverbal skills. She meets criteria for continued speech-language intervention services.

8. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Majo is recommended for ongoing speech-language intervention services, with a transition from Western Piedmont CDSA Infant-Toddler Program services to preschool-based services coordinated through the local school system, to begin no later than her third birthday equivalent eligibility window closes (CPT 92523 recommended for the combined speech sound and language re-evaluation at time of transition).

2. Intervention should address both Spanish and English, with primary emphasis on Spanish given current home language dominance, in order to support Majo's communication across all environments, including with doña Lupe at home and with Miss Ana and la maestra Carmen at school and daycare.

3. Target areas for speech sound intervention should include final consonant production, consonant cluster production, and liquid production (/l/, /r/) in both languages, moving from min cues toward independent production across increasingly complex contexts.

4. Target areas for language intervention should include expansion of mean length of utterance, use of grammatical morphemes (plurals, verb tense) in both languages, and multi-step direction-following, consistent with classroom demands reported by Majo's teachers.

5. The family is encouraged to continue providing rich language input in Spanish, including through shared book reading, narrating daily routines, and expanding on Majo's utterances, and to share strategies learned in therapy with doña Lupe and Mr. Tom given their regular caregiving roles.

6. Majo's teachers, Miss Ana and la maestra Carmen, are encouraged to continue providing visual supports and simplified, repeated directions during classroom routines, and to coordinate with the eventual preschool-based SLP regarding classroom carryover strategies.

7. Continued monitoring of middle ear status is recommended given Majo's history of recurrent otitis media; any recurrence of fluid or hearing changes should be promptly evaluated by Dr. Rebecca Simmons or an audiologist, with results shared with the treating SLP.

8. Re-evaluation of speech and language skills is recommended in approximately 6 months, or sooner if significant changes in status or classroom placement occur, to monitor progress and adjust service recommendations as Majo transitions into her new preschool placement.

This evaluation and these recommendations were discussed with Mrs. López and doña Lupe in Spanish, with interpreter support from Gloria Reyes, at the conclusion of the session. A written summary will also be forwarded to Whitney Brooks at Western Piedmont CDSA and to Dr. Rebecca Simmons's office with the family's consent.

Respectfully submitted,

Jennifer Hayes, M.S., CCC-SLP
Licensed Speech-Language Pathologist
Carolina Bilingual Speech & Language Services, PLLC

Motivo de la referencia

María José fue referida al CDSA del Condado de Durham el 12 de enero de 2025 a raíz de una preocupación expresada por su pediatra, Dr. Michael Chen, durante la visita de control de los 3 años en Pediatría Asociada de Durham. Su mamá, Alejandra Castillo Reyes, reportó que Majo usaba muy pocas palabras combinadas y que personas fuera del hogar con frecuencia no entendían lo que decía. La familia también fue referida por la nutricionista del programa WIC, quien notó un vocabulario limitado durante una cita de rutina en febrero de 2025. Tras el proceso de elegibilidad, María José fue encontrada elegible para servicios de intervención temprana bajo la Parte C, y se programó esta evaluación integral de habla y lenguaje para informar el Plan Individualizado de Servicios para la Familia (IFSP).

La evaluación se realizó en el hogar familiar el 3 de junio de 2025, con la participación de Alejandra Castillo Reyes y, por teléfono durante parte de la sesión, Ricardo Fernández Soto, quien se encontraba en su turno de trabajo. La examinadora, Katherine Simmons, es bilingüe en español e inglés y condujo toda la evaluación en español, el idioma predominante del hogar.

Antecedentes de nacimiento y desarrollo

María José nació a las 38 semanas de gestación por parto vaginal en el Hospital Regional de Durham el 14/03/2022, con un peso de 6 libras 8 onzas. El embarazo fue descrito por Alejandra Castillo Reyes como sin complicaciones, aunque mencionó náuseas severas durante el primer trimestre que requirieron una visita a la sala de emergencias. No se reportaron complicaciones durante el parto ni estancia prolongada en la unidad neonatal. Majo recibió el alta hospitalaria junto con su madre a las 48 horas de vida.

El historial médico de María José incluye otitis media recurrente, con tres episodios documentados entre los 8 de octubre de 2023 y los 20 de enero de 2024. Fue vista por un otorrinolaringólogo, el Dr. Samuel Patel, en Especialistas de Oído, Nariz y Garganta del Triángulo, quien colocó tubos de ventilación bilaterales el 2 de febrero de 2024. Desde ese procedimiento, la madre reporta una reducción notable en la frecuencia de infecciones de oído. Una evaluación audiológica de seguimiento realizada el 15 de abril de 2025 mostró audición dentro de límites normales en ambos oídos.

No se reportan antecedentes de convulsiones, hospitalizaciones por causas distintas a las mencionadas, cirugías mayores, ni alergias alimentarias conocidas. María José toma vitaminas infantiles de venta libre pero no otros medicamentos de manera regular. Su visión fue evaluada como normal durante el examen pediátrico más reciente.

En cuanto a los hitos del desarrollo motor, la madre reporta que Majo se sentó sin apoyo alrededor de los 7 meses y caminó de manera independiente a los 14 meses, ambos dentro de los rangos esperados. Las habilidades motoras finas también se describen como apropiadas para la edad; la niña dibuja garabatos circulares, usa cubiertos con supervisión mínima y puede apilar seis a ocho bloques.

Historia familiar y del lenguaje

María José vive con su madre, Alejandra Castillo Reyes; su padre, Ricardo Fernández Soto; y su hermano mayor, Diego Fernández Castillo, de 8 años. Alejandra Castillo Reyes trabaja de noche en Empacadora Avícola Carolina del Piamonte, en el turno de las 11:00 p.m. a las 7:00 a.m., mientras que Ricardo Fernández Soto trabaja durante el día como operario en Grupo de Construcción Triángulo. Debido al horario nocturno de la madre, la abuela materna, Rosa Castillo, cuida a María José y a Diego tres noches por semana mientras Alejandra trabaja y Ricardo duerme antes de su propio turno.

El español es el idioma principal del hogar; ambos padres y Rosa Castillo se dirigen a los niños casi exclusivamente en español. Diego asiste a segundo grado en Escuela Primaria Holt y es bilingüe, alternando entre español en casa e inglés en la escuela. Alejandra Castillo Reyes reporta que Diego con frecuencia traduce para la familia en citas médicas cuando el personal no habla español.

No se reportan antecedentes familiares de trastornos del habla, el lenguaje o el aprendizaje en ninguno de los dos lados de la familia, aunque la madre menciona que un primo materno, al que la familia llama simplemente "el primo de Rosa," tuvo retraso en el habla de niño y recibió terapia escolar.

María José asiste a Pequeños Pasos Daycare cuatro días a la semana, de 8:00 a.m. a 4:00 p.m., en un salón bilingüe dirigido por la Srta. Jennifer Hall. La Srta. Hall reporta que Majo es sociable y busca jugar con sus compañeros, en particular con una niña llamada Emily, pero que su habla con frecuencia es difícil de entender incluso para los adultos que la conocen bien. En casa, a María José le gusta jugar con el perro de la familia, Max, y pasar tiempo viendo videos infantiles en español en una tableta.

La familia también recibe apoyo de Smart Start del Condado de Durham, que subsidia parte del costo de la guardería, y continúa participando en el programa WIC para servicios de nutrición.

Procedimientos de evaluación y comportamiento durante la prueba

La evaluación incluyó observación informal, entrevista a los padres, revisión de expedientes, y la administración de pruebas estandarizadas e informales. María José se mostró inicialmente tímida pero se calentó rápidamente al juego y participó de manera activa durante la mayor parte de la sesión, de aproximadamente 90 minutos. Se tomaron descansos cortos para mantener su atención, y las últimas tareas se completaron con apoyo adicional de refuerzo mediante pegatinas.

Resultados de las pruebas

Rossetti Infant-Toddler Language Scale: Esta escala de desarrollo del lenguaje, administrada mediante observación estructurada y reporte materno, evaluó las áreas de interacción-apego, pragmática, gestos, comprensión del lenguaje y expresión del lenguaje. María José obtuvo desempeños dentro del rango esperado en interacción-apego, pragmática y gestos, pero mostró retraso significativo en comprensión y, de manera más marcada, en expresión del lenguaje.

Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation-3 (adaptado informalmente al español con transcripción fonética): Se evaluó la producción de consonantes en posición inicial, media y final de palabra. María José mostró procesos fonológicos consistentes con reducción de grupos consonánticos (por ejemplo, "pato" por "plato"), frontalización velar (produciendo [t] por /k/ en palabras como "casa"), y omisión de consonantes finales. Se observaron además sustituciones de líquidas, con /l/ y /r/ con frecuencia sustituidas por [j] o omitidas, como en su producción de "aguia" por "[k]aguja" y "bano" para "guante" lo cual refleja omisión de la consonante inicial con cambios adicionales.

Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test-5 (forma en español, administración informal con apoyo visual): Esta prueba evaluó el vocabulario receptivo mediante la selección de imágenes correspondientes a palabras habladas.

Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development-4, Subescala de Comunicación: Se administraron ítems seleccionados de esta subescala para corroborar el funcionamiento comunicativo observado en otras medidas.

Resultados estandarizados:
Prueba	Área evaluada	Puntaje estándar	Percentil	Edad equivalente
Rossetti Infant-Toddler Language Scale	Comprensión	No estandarizado	N/A	18-20 meses
Rossetti Infant-Toddler Language Scale	Expresión	No estandarizado	N/A	14-16 meses
Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation-3	Inteligibilidad de sonidos	71	3	2;4
Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test-5	Vocabulario receptivo	74	4	2;6
Bayley-4 (ítems seleccionados)	Comunicación	79	8	2;8

Durante la muestra de lenguaje espontáneo, María José produjo un promedio de 2.1 palabras por enunciado, con un rango de 1 a 3 palabras. Entre sus producciones se registraron: "mami agua" (solicitando agua), "no quiero" (rechazando una actividad), y "Diego pelota" (comentando sobre su hermano). El inventario fonético consonántico incluyó /p, b, m, n, t, d/ de manera consistente, con producción inconsistente de /k, g, f, s/ y ausencia casi total de /l, r, ɾ/ y de grupos consonánticos. La inteligibilidad para oyentes no familiares se estimó en aproximadamente 30%, y para oyentes familiares en aproximadamente 60%, con apoyo de contexto.

Se observó un vocabulario expresivo estimado de menos de 50 palabras según reporte materno, con uso emergente pero inconsistente de combinaciones de dos palabras. No se observaron dificultades en la comprensión de instrucciones simples de un solo paso dentro de contexto, pero instrucciones de dos pasos sin apoyo gestual resultaron en respuestas inconsistentes.

Las habilidades pragmáticas, incluyendo contacto visual, toma de turnos, atención conjunta y uso de gestos comunicativos, se observaron dentro de límites apropiados para la edad y constituyen una fortaleza relativa importante.

Impresiones clínicas

Con base en los resultados de esta evaluación, las observaciones clínicas y el reporte de los padres y de la maestra, María José Fernández Castillo presenta un retraso en el desarrollo del lenguaje tanto receptivo como expresivo, de moderado a severo, junto con un trastorno fonológico que afecta significativamente su inteligibilidad. Los patrones fonológicos observados, incluyendo la reducción de grupos consonánticos, la frontalización velar y la omisión de consonantes finales, son consistentes con un retraso en el desarrollo fonológico más allá de lo esperado para su edad cronológica de 3;2, incluso considerando la exposición bilingüe del hogar.

El perfil de María José no parece explicarse únicamente por diferencia dialectal o por la exposición a dos idiomas; su hermano, Diego Fernández Castillo, según reporte materno, no presentó patrones similares a esta edad. Las fortalezas relativas en atención conjunta, gestos comunicativos e interacción social son un buen pronóstico para la respuesta a la intervención directa.

El historial de otitis media recurrente documentado entre octubre de 2023 y enero de 2024 pudo haber contribuido al retraso observado, aunque la audición actual se documenta como normal según la evaluación audiológica del 15 de abril de 2025.

Recomendaciones

1. Se recomienda que María José reciba terapia de habla y lenguaje individual dos veces por semana, con sesiones de 45 minutos, enfocadas en la expansión del vocabulario expresivo, el aumento de la longitud del enunciado y la reducción de los procesos fonológicos identificados.
2. Se recomienda que los servicios se provean en español, el idioma dominante del hogar, por un proveedor bilingüe certificado.
3. Se recomienda consulta de seguimiento con audiología cada seis meses dado el historial de otitis media recurrente.
4. Se recomienda que la familia reciba materiales de apoyo en español para facilitar prácticas de lenguaje en el hogar, incluyendo estrategias para Alejandra Castillo Reyes, Ricardo Fernández Soto y Rosa Castillo, dado el rol activo de esta última en el cuidado diario de María José.
5. Se recomienda coordinación con la Srta. Jennifer Hall en Pequeños Pasos Daycare para la implementación de estrategias de apoyo al lenguaje dentro del salón de clases.
6. Se recomienda reevaluación formal antes de la transición del programa de intervención temprana del Part C, aproximadamente a los 3 años 6 meses de edad.

Se discutieron estos resultados y recomendaciones con Alejandra Castillo Reyes el día de la evaluación, y se le proporcionó un resumen verbal en español. Se compartirá una copia completa de este informe con la familia, con el Dr. Michael Chen en Pediatría Asociada de Durham, y con el equipo del IFSP en la reunión programada para el 24 de junio de 2025.

La próxima revisión del IFSP está programada para el 03/12/2025, seis meses después del inicio de servicios, para evaluar el progreso y ajustar las metas según sea necesario.

text:
TRIANGLE PEDIATRIC THERAPY, PLLC  —  SPEECH-LANGUAGE EVALUATION REPORT

Client Name: Mateo Hernández Cruz  Preferred Name: Teo  Date of Birth: 14/01/2022  Chronological Age: 4;2
Evaluation Date(s): 3 de marzo de 2025 and 03/10/2025  Report Date: March 14, 2025
Medicaid ID: 7482913605K  Case/Record ID: CDSA-NC-00417-25
Parent/Guardian: Lucía Hernández  Address: 418 Possum Trot Road, Garner, NC 27529
Home Phone: (919) 555-2847  Cell Phone: (919) 555-0163  Email: lucia.hernandez85@gmail.com
Referring Source: Dr. Angela Kim, pediatrician, Garner Children's Clinic
Evaluating Clinician: Jennifer Walsh, M.S., CCC-SLP, Triangle Pediatric Therapy, PLLC
Interpreter: Mr. Rivera, Spanish language line, certified medical interpreter
Service Coordinator: Patricia Nguyen, Wake County CDSA
Primary Languages: Spanish (home) and English (daycare)  Language of Report: English

REASON FOR REFERRAL

Mateo is a 4-year, 2-month-old bilingual Spanish/English-speaking boy who was referred for a comprehensive speech-language evaluation by Dr. Kim after Teo's mother, Lucía Hernández, expressed concern that his speech is difficult for unfamiliar listeners to understand and that he is not yet combining words the way his older sister did at the same age. Ms. Lopez, Mateo's teacher at Little Sprouts Daycare, also raised concerns in a note sent home on el martes 4 de marzo de 2025, noting that Mateo often points or gestures instead of using words during circle time in Ms. Lopez's room. This evaluation was requested to determine Mateo's current speech and language skills in both languages, to clarify whether a delay exists, and to make recommendations for services.

BACKGROUND INFORMATION

Mateo lives with his mother, Lucía Hernández; his father, Carlos Hernández; his older sister, Camila, age 7; and his younger brother, Diego, age 1, at the family's home on Possum Trot Road in Garner. The family's dog, Rocky, is frequently mentioned by Mateo during play. Lucía reports that she was born and raised in the village of El Rosario, in the department of Olancho, Honduras, and moved to the United States in 2014. Carlos grew up in Siguatepeque, Honduras, and immigrated in 2012. Both parents are fluent Spanish speakers; Lucía reports conversational English and Carlos reports limited English proficiency. Carlos works full time at Carolina Poultry Processors on the second shift, from 3:00 p.m. to 11:30 p.m., which affects the amount of time he spends with Mateo on weekdays.

Mateo's maternal grandmother, Rosa Morales, lives nearby and picks him up from daycare most afternoons around 4:30 p.m., caring for him until Lucía returns from work at approximately 6:15 p.m.. A family friend, Yolanda Pérez, occasionally babysits on weekends. Lucía reports that Rosa speaks only Spanish with Mateo, while Camila often speaks to him in a mix of English and Spanish.

BIRTH AND MEDICAL HISTORY

Mateo was born on 14/01/2022 at WakeMed Raleigh Campus following a full-term pregnancy and uncomplicated vaginal delivery. Birth weight was reported as 7 lbs 4 oz, and Lucía reports no complications during the pregnancy, labor, or delivery. Mateo passed his newborn hearing screening prior to discharge. Developmental milestones were reported as follows: sat independently around 6 months, walked independently around 13 months, and said his first words around 15 months. Lucía reports that Mateo's expressive vocabulary growth slowed noticeably after age 2, around the time his brother Diego was born.

Medical history is significant for recurrent otitis media. Mateo had his first documented ear infection at approximately 18 months and has had at least five additional episodes since, most recently treated in enero de 2025. Dr. Kim's office referred Mateo to an ENT, Dr. Samuel Ortiz, who placed bilateral pressure-equalization tubes on 02/18/2024. A follow-up audiological evaluation completed on 09/05/2024 at UNC Children's Audiology indicated hearing within normal limits bilaterally, with normal tympanometry at that time. Mateo's vision screening at his most recent well-child visit on 03/01/2025 was within normal limits. No diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder, seizure disorder, or genetic syndrome has been made. Mateo is not currently taking any medications. He is up to date on immunizations per his pediatrician's records.

FAMILY AND LANGUAGE HISTORY

Lucía reports that Spanish is the primary language spoken in the home among all family members, with the exception of Camila, who frequently code-switches into English, particularly when discussing school or cartoons. Lucía estimates that Mateo hears approximately 80% Spanish and 20% English at home, and the reverse proportion while at daycare. She reports that Mateo's receptive skills in Spanish appear stronger than his receptive skills in English, and that he responds more readily to directions given by Rosa in Spanish than to directions given by Ms. Lopez in English.

Lucía reports a family history of speech and language concerns: Rosa, Mateo's grandmother, states that Carlos himself had delayed speech as a child in Siguatepeque and did not begin combining words until close to age 4, though he received no formal intervention. Lucía denies any other family history of speech, language, hearing, or learning concerns on her side of the family.

Mateo has attended Little Sprouts Daycare, located at 2210 Timber Drive in Garner, since August 2023. He is currently enrolled in Ms. Lopez's room, a mixed 3- to 4-year-old classroom with fourteen children. Ms. Lopez reports that Mateo plays well alongside peers, particularly a classmate named Sofia, but rarely initiates verbal interaction and instead relies on gestures, pulling, and pointing to communicate his needs. Ms. Lopez reports that during circle time, which runs from 9:15 a.m. to 9:45 a.m. each morning, Mateo participates in songs and movement activities but does not yet sing along with recognizable words.

DEVELOPMENTAL AND EDUCATIONAL HISTORY

Lucía first raised concerns about Mateo's speech with Dr. Kim at his 2-year well-child visit. At that time, watch-and-wait was recommended. Concerns persisted, and at the 3-year well-child visit on 15/01/2025, Dr. Kim referred the family to Wake County CDSA for evaluation. Mateo was found eligible for early intervention services under the category of communication delay, and an Individualized Family Service Plan (IFSP) was developed on el 4 de febrero de 2025, with a six-month review scheduled for 04/08/2025. Patricia Nguyen, the family's service coordinator through Wake County CDSA, has been involved in coordinating this evaluation and will receive a copy of this report for the IFSP team.

The family has also received support from Smart Start of Wake County, which connected Lucía with a parenting class focused on bilingual language stimulation strategies, attended on 20/02/2025.

ASSESSMENT PROCEDURES

This evaluation was conducted across two sessions at the Triangle Pediatric Therapy, PLLC clinic. The first session took place on 3 de marzo de 2025 from 10:00 a.m. to 11:15 a.m. and consisted of parent interview, hearing screening, oral-motor examination, and administration of English standardized measures. The second session took place on 03/10/2025 from 2:30 p.m. to 3:45 p.m. and consisted of administration of Spanish standardized measures, a bilingual language sample, and a speech sound sample in both languages, with interpretation support provided by Mr. Rivera for parent report items.

Procedures included a parent interview and case history review, an oral-peripheral examination, a pure-tone hearing screening (passed bilaterally at 20 dB HL for 1000, 2000, and 4000 Hz), administration of standardized assessments in English and Spanish, dynamic assessment of bilingual language sampling, and clinical observation across both testing sessions and in Ms. Lopez's classroom during an informal observation on March 7, 2025 from 9:00 a.m. to 9:30 a.m..

STANDARDIZED TEST RESULTS

Assessment                                              Language    Standard Score    Percentile Rank
Preschool Language Scales–5 (PLS-5), Auditory Comprehension    English     82             12th
Preschool Language Scales–5 (PLS-5), Expressive Communication   English     74              4th
Preschool Language Scales–5 (PLS-5), Total Language Score       English     77              6th
Bilingual English Spanish Assessment (BESA), Morphosyntax       Spanish     88             21st
Bilingual English Spanish Assessment (BESA), Semantics          Spanish     91             27th
Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation–3 (GFTA-3)                 English     71              3rd
Clinical Assessment of Articulation and Phonology–Spanish       Spanish     85             16th

On the PLS-5, Mateo's Expressive Communication score fell in the moderately delayed range, while Auditory Comprehension fell in the mildly delayed range. On the BESA, administered to evaluate Mateo's skills relative to other bilingual children with similar language exposure, his Morphosyntax and Semantics scores fell within the low average range, suggesting that his language skills in Spanish, his dominant home language, are closer to age expectations than his English scores alone would suggest. Composite scores combining both languages were not calculated, consistent with best practice for sequential bilingual learners at this stage of English exposure.

On the GFTA-3, Mateo produced numerous sound errors affecting intelligibility, including stopping of fricatives, gliding of liquids, and final consonant deletion. He produced "tat" for "cat," "doo" for "shoe," and "ba" for "ball." On the Spanish articulation measure, error patterns were largely consistent with those observed in English, including difficulty with the trilled /r/, substitution of [d] for /ɾ/ in words such as "pero," and cluster reduction in words like "fruta" produced as "futa." These error patterns were judged to reflect a true speech sound disorder rather than typical second-language transfer, given their presence across both languages and their inconsistency with developmental norms for his age in either language.

LANGUAGE SAMPLE

A 20-minute bilingual play-based language sample was collected using toy animals, a dollhouse, and a set of vehicles, with Mateo's mother present to support elicitation in Spanish and the clinician eliciting in English. Mateo's mean length of utterance (MLU) in morphemes was calculated at 2.1 in English and 2.6 in Spanish, both below age expectations of approximately 3.5–4.5 morphemes for a child his age. SALT coding of the transcript indicated frequent [EW] (error word) codes associated with omitted grammatical morphemes, including omission of articles, copula "is/es," and plural markers in both languages. Mateo used primarily single words and two-word combinations such as "más agua," "no quiero," and "Teo jugar," with few examples of three-word utterances observed. He demonstrated use of present-tense verbs but did not use past-tense marking in either language during the sample.

Pragmatically, Mateo demonstrated joint attention, turn-taking during simple games, and functional use of gestures to request and comment. He made eye contact appropriately and responded to his name consistently. He engaged in brief back-and-forth exchanges with the clinician when supported with visual cues and modeling, and his mother reported that this behavior was consistent with how he interacts with Rosa and Camila at home.

ORAL-PERIPHERAL EXAMINATION

Structures and function of the lips, tongue, hard and soft palate, and jaw were assessed and found to be within normal limits for structure and symmetry. Diadochokinetic rates were judged appropriate for age. No signs of dysarthria or apraxia of speech were observed, although mild inconsistency in sound production across repeated trials of multisyllabic words was noted and will be monitored.

HEARING SCREENING

Mateo passed a bilateral pure-tone hearing screening at 20 dB HL across 1000, 2000, and 4000 Hz, consistent with his most recent audiological evaluation on 09/05/2024. Given his history of recurrent otitis media, ongoing monitoring of hearing status is recommended, including tympanometry at future pediatric visits.

CLINICAL IMPRESSIONS

Based on parent report, teacher report, standardized test results, and clinical observation, Mateo presents with a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder (ICD-10: F80.2) affecting both Spanish and English, along with a speech sound disorder (ICD-10: F80.0) affecting intelligibility in both languages. His language delay cannot be attributed solely to bilingual exposure, as deficits are evident relative to same-age bilingual peers on a measure normed for bilingual children (BESA) as well as on English-only measures. His speech sound errors are consistent across both languages and exceed what would be expected from typical cross-linguistic transfer or second-language acquisition at this stage.

Mateo's history of recurrent otitis media, while not currently associated with a measurable hearing loss, may have contributed to early language learning difficulty and should continue to be monitored closely given the established relationship between chronic middle ear effusion and speech-language development in young children.

Mateo demonstrates relative strengths in nonverbal communication, joint attention, play skills, and social engagement, which are positive prognostic indicators for therapy. His home language environment, which includes consistent Spanish input from his mother and grandmother, should be supported and maintained rather than discouraged, consistent with current evidence-based practice for bilingual children with communication disorders.

RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Mateo is recommended for speech-language therapy services twice weekly for 30-minute individual sessions, targeting both expressive language development and speech sound production, with services provided bilingually or with interpreter support as needed.
2. Therapy goals should address morphosyntactic development (plural markers, verb tense marking, article use) in both Spanish and English, expansion of utterance length toward age-appropriate MLU, and remediation of speech sound errors including stopping, gliding, final consonant deletion, and liquid/rhotic errors.
3. Continued coordination with Wake County CDSA and service coordinator Patricia Nguyen is recommended to incorporate these findings into Mateo's IFSP at the upcoming review scheduled for 04/08/2025.
4. Collaboration with Ms. Lopez and Little Sprouts Daycare staff is recommended to implement classroom-based language stimulation strategies and to monitor Mateo's participation during structured activities such as circle time.
5. The family is encouraged to continue providing rich Spanish language input at home and to consider structured bilingual storybook reading in the evening, for example between 7:00 p.m. and 7:30 p.m. before Mateo's bedtime routine, as a low-pressure opportunity for vocabulary and narrative exposure.
6. Continued audiological monitoring is recommended given Mateo's history of recurrent otitis media, including follow-up tympanometry at his next pediatric visit with Dr. Kim.
7. Re-evaluation of speech and language skills is recommended in approximately six months, or sooner if concerns change, to monitor progress and adjust the treatment plan.

Mateo's parents, Lucía Hernández and Carlos Hernández, were present for discussion of results at the conclusion of the second session and voiced agreement with the recommendations above. Questions may be directed to the undersigned clinician at Triangle Pediatric Therapy, PLLC, (919) 555-7720, or jwalsh@trianglepeds-slp.com.

Respectfully submitted,

Jennifer Walsh, M.S., CCC-SLP
Bilingual Speech-Language Pathologist
Triangle Pediatric Therapy, PLLC
Report completed: March 14, 2025

text:
+ Name: María José Hernández López
+ DOB: March 3, 2024 (also recorded by family as 3 de marzo de 2024)
+ CA: 2;7
+ Context: Six-Month IFSP Review Meeting, Piedmont Regional CDSA office, Hillsborough, NC
+ Clinician: Mrinoy Banerjee, M.S., CCC-SLP, bilingual speech-language pathologist, contracted through Triangle Bilingual Therapy Associates
+ Service Coordinator: Denise Calloway, Piedmont Regional CDSA
+ Interpreter: Rosa Fuentes (Spanish/English), present for family portions of the meeting
+ Date of Review: el martes 4 de junio de 2026 (also 06/04/2026, 2026-06-04)
+ Date of Prior IFSP: 12/08/2025
+ Date of Last Evaluation: November 19, 2025
+ Record/Case ID: CDSA-2024-00871
+ Medicaid ID: 987654321A

Summary: This Six-Month IFSP Review was held for María José, a 2;7 bilingual (Spanish/English) toddler referred to Piedmont Regional CDSA for delayed expressive and receptive language, limited intelligible speech, and oral-motor concerns noted by her pediatrician, Dr. Anand Patel. The meeting reviewed progress on current outcomes, updated family concerns and priorities, and revised strategies for home, Sunshine Bilingual Daycare, and direct SLP services. María José's mother, Lucía Hernández Reyes, and father, Javier López Morales, attended in person; her maternal grandmother participated by phone from outside the country. Standardized assessment and ongoing progress monitoring were discussed using the Rossetti Infant-Toddler Language Scale, the Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation-3, the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development-4, and the Peabody Developmental Motor Scales-3.

**Family Background**

María José Hernández López lives with her parents, Lucía Hernández Reyes and Javier López Morales, and her older brother, Diego, age 5, at 412 Willowbrook Lane, Hillsborough, NC 27278, in Orange County. The family dog, Luna, is frequently mentioned by Lucía as a source of motivation during play-based practice, since María José enjoys calling Luna by name. Javier works full-time at a Food Lion distribution center in Mebane, and Lucía is the primary caregiver during the day. María José's maternal grandmother, Rosario Reyes de Hernández, lives in Quetzaltenango, Guatemala and was connected to the meeting by phone at +502 5512-3456 to provide input on family routines and cultural priorities, since she assists remotely with childcare advice and was present for the birth of both children during visits.

The family's primary contact numbers are (919) 555-0148 (mother's cell), 919.555.0199 (father's cell), and 1-800-555-0123 for the CDSA main line. A secondary contact for Lucía's cousin in Mexico City, who sometimes assists with translation of written materials, is +52 55 1234 5678. Lucía stated she prefers texts over calls during work hours for Javier, but the home number 919-555-0177 is best for reaching her directly.

**Concerns and Priorities**

In the family's own words, Lucía shared, through interpreter Rosa Fuentes: "Queremos que María José pueda decirnos lo que necesita sin frustrarse. Ella entiende todo, pero no le salen las palabras." Javier added: "Nos preocupa que en la guardería no la entiendan y que eso la haga sentir sola." The family's top priorities, ranked during the review, were: (1) increasing intelligible word combinations in both languages, (2) reducing frustration-related tantrums when María José is not understood, (3) supporting turn-taking and play skills with her brother Diego and with peers at Sunshine Bilingual Daycare, and (4) continuing bilingual input at home so María José does not lose Spanish while gaining English.

Lucía noted that extended family visits, including a planned trip to see Rosario in Guatemala over the winter holidays, are important and that the family wants strategies that travel well and don't require special equipment.

**Daily Routines**

María José's typical day begins around 7:00 a.m. with breakfast at home, followed by drop-off at Sunshine Bilingual Daycare in Hillsborough by 7:45 a.m.. Her lead teacher there, Ms. Carla Alvarez, reports that María José engages well with toys but uses mostly gestures and a handful of approximated words to communicate with classmates, including her favorite playmate, Soleil. Lunch is at 11:30 a.m., followed by a nap, and pickup by Lucía or occasionally her aunt, Marisol Reyes, around 4:30 p.m.. Evenings include bath time, a bilingual story routine led by Javier in Spanish and English, and bedtime by 8:00 p.m.. Lucía described mealtime as the hardest part of the day, since María José often points or pulls at her mother's sleeve instead of requesting foods by name, which increases frustration for both of them.

**Other Agencies Involved**

The family currently receives support from WIC for nutrition services and has an open case with Orange County DSS for childcare subsidy. Lucía also attends a parenting group through Smart Start of Orange County on Thursday mornings. María José's pediatric care continues with Dr. Anand Patel at UNC Children's Clinic in Chapel Hill, who referred the family for the original evaluation after a 12-month well-child visit raised concerns about expressive language delay. No hearing or feeding concerns have been identified; a hearing screening was completed and passed at UNC Children's Clinic on January 14, 2026.

**Assessment Results**

At the most recent evaluation on November 19, 2025, María José was administered the Rossetti Infant-Toddler Language Scale in both English and Spanish, with receptive language scoring in the 25th percentile and expressive language scoring in the 9th percentile relative to same-age peers, consistent with a significant expressive delay and borderline receptive delay. The Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development-4 yielded a Cognitive composite standard score of 95 and a Language composite standard score of 76, with the Expressive Communication subtest falling more than 2 standard deviations below the mean. The Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation-3 was attempted informally given her limited expressive output; stimulability for /p/, /t/, and [w] was noted, but /k/ was consistently produced as [t], and final consonants were frequently omitted, coded as [EW] on several single-word attempts. The Peabody Developmental Motor Scales-3 indicated age-appropriate fine and gross motor skills, ruling out motor-based explanations for the oral-motor patterns observed.

During today's review, informal language sampling showed continued gains: María José produced spontaneous two-word combinations in both languages, including "más leche," glossed as [tete], and "no quiero," approximately 8 out of 10 attempts intelligible to familiar listeners, up from roughly 40% intelligibility at the prior IFSP. Her diagnosis remains consistent with Developmental Language Disorder (ICD-10 F80.1), and current services are billed under CPT 92523 for combined speech sound and language evaluation, with ongoing treatment billed under CPT 92507.

**Current Outcomes and Progress**

*Outcome 1: María José will use two- to three-word combinations to request preferred items and comment during play, in English and/or Spanish, across home and daycare settings.*
Progress: Met with modification. María José now produces two-word combinations with moderate verbal cues (mod cues) in structured play and occasionally spontaneously during snack time. Strategy updates include continued use of bilingual self-talk and parallel talk by Lucía, Javier, and Ms. Alvarez, along with a core vocabulary board introduced for daycare use.

*Outcome 2: María José will reduce frustration behaviors (hitting, crying, throwing objects) when communication breakdowns occur, as reported by caregivers.*
Progress: Partially met. Frequency of tantrums has decreased from several times daily to roughly 2 to 3 times per week per parent report. Strategy updates include teaching a simple sign for "help" and expanding the use of visual choice boards at home and at Sunshine Bilingual Daycare.

*Outcome 3: María José will engage in reciprocal play routines with Diego and peers, taking at least two turns in a shared activity.*
Progress: Emerging. María José now tolerates longer joint attention during turn-taking games with Diego and has begun initiating simple games with Soleil at daycare. Strategy updates include structured turn-taking games (rolling a ball, stacking blocks) modeled by Mrinoy Banerjee during sessions and generalized at home.

*Outcome 4: The family will report increased confidence in supporting bilingual language development at home.*
Progress: Met. Lucía and Javier both report feeling more comfortable using strategies learned in coaching sessions, including expansion, repetition, and wait time, in both Spanish and English. Rosario has also begun using similar strategies during video calls from Guatemala.

**New and Revised Outcomes**

Given the progress noted above, the team revised Outcome 1 to target three- to four-word combinations and added a new outcome focused on articulation of final consonants, targeting words such as "pan," "sol," and "gato," using minimal pairs and auditory bombardment. The team also added a new outcome supporting María José's participation in small-group activities at Sunshine Bilingual Daycare with no more than moderate cues from adults by the next review.

**Service Delivery**

Direct speech-language services will continue at a frequency of one 45-minute session weekly, split between the family's home and Sunshine Bilingual Daycare, provided by Mrinoy Banerjee through Triangle Bilingual Therapy Associates under contract with Piedmont Regional CDSA. Service coordination continues monthly with Denise Calloway. The family requested that at least one session per month occur in the late afternoon, around 4:00 p.m., to accommodate Javier's schedule, and the team agreed to alternate session times accordingly.

The next formal evaluation is scheduled for December 1, 2026, with the following annual IFSP meeting tentatively set for el 8 de diciembre de 2026. A brief check-in call with the family is planned for 09/15/2026 to review progress on the new articulation outcome prior to the family's travel to Guatemala.

**Signatures and Consent**

Lucía Hernández Reyes and Javier López Morales both signed consent for continued services and agreed to the outcomes and strategies outlined above. Denise Calloway confirmed that transportation and interpretation supports remain in place for all future visits. Rosa Fuentes will continue to be scheduled for all family-facing meetings. Contact information was reconfirmed as (919) 555-0148 for Lucía and 919.555.0199 for Javier, with lucia.hernandez0871@example.com added as a secondary contact for written communications from Piedmont Regional CDSA. The family's CDSA portal account can be accessed at https://portal.piedmontcdsa.example.org/families/987654321A for review of documents between visits.

This review was completed collaboratively by Mrinoy Banerjee, Denise Calloway, Rosa Fuentes, and the family, with input gathered from Ms. Carla Alvarez by phone prior to the meeting and from Rosario Reyes de Hernández during the meeting itself. All parties agreed that progress has been meaningful over the past six months and that the revised outcomes reflect María José's emerging strengths in both English and Spanish communication.
